scope_spec.original_topic:
Write the first two chapters of a narrative review on AI-enabled nanobiosensing for cancer therapy.

Central question: How does AI contribute to sensor design and interpretation, and how reliably can these systems identify anticancer drugs and characterize exposure across biological matrices and time?

Investigate this question without assuming that AI improves every sensor or that laboratory performance establishes clinical usefulness.

The structure, section questions, word targets and instructions are in the outline supplied with this run (input/outline.json).
scope_spec.normalized_topic: The first two chapters of a narrative review examining AI contributions to nanosensor and probe design, molecular recognition and signal interpretation, followed by the reliability of anticancer-drug identification, concentration estimation, nanomedicine measurement and temporal exposure assessment across biological matrices, without presuming AI superiority or clinical usefulness.
scope_spec.central_question: How does AI contribute to sensor design and interpretation, and how reliably can these systems identify anticancer drugs and characterize exposure across biological matrices and time?
scope_spec.audience: Non-specialist scientific readers, including researchers, educators and policymakers across fields; define sensing, machine-learning and pharmacokinetic terminology at first use.

in_scope: The supplied S1 and S2 chapters, with their eight subsections retained as the primary themes.
AI-assisted selection or optimization of sensing materials, surface chemistry, recognition elements, probe sequences, array components, fabrication and measurement conditions.

Learned interpretation of optical, Raman, multisensor-array, electrochemical and repeated nanosensor measurements, including the connection between sensing interactions, signals, model inputs and outputs.
Analytical performance, predictive performance, independent evaluation units and generalization across samples, individuals, matrices, batches and time.
Identification and quantification of anticancer drugs, distinguishing presence detection, identity classification, concentration categories and numerical concentration estimates.
Experiments in buffer, synthetic biofluids, spiked biological specimens and specimens collected after administration, kept as separate evidence settings.
Nanomedicine measurements distinguishing carrier-associated signals, intact carriers, payload, encapsulated or released drug, release-related changes and distribution.
Serial, continuous and near-continuous measurements, pharmacokinetic estimation and temporal prediction, with measured and modeled quantities distinguished.
Limitations on interpreting sampled concentrations as biological exposure, including matrix interference, reference measurements, transferability and sampled-compartment versus tumour exposure.
Methodological and simpler analytical comparators directly relevant to the included sensing tasks.
out_of_scope: Later chapters on treatment response, toxicity and treatment decisions, including detailed treatment selection or dose-adjustment strategies.
Drug-delivery or formulation design without a directly evaluated sensing function.
General AI for oncology, drug discovery, molecular docking or pharmacokinetic prediction without a substantive connection to the included sensing systems.
Conventional non-nanoscale sensors as standalone coverage; directly relevant comparator or methodological context may be retained.
Cancer diagnosis or biomarker discovery as standalone applications without a direct contribution to the Chapter 1 design, recognition, signal-interpretation or evaluation questions.

Claims that a predictive fingerprint establishes biological mechanism, that a carrier label establishes released payload, or that laboratory performance establishes clinical utility without supporting evidence.

perspective_options.angle: The researcher-defined review examines what AI contributes to nanosensor design and interpretation and which evaluation conditions justify drug-identification and exposure claims.
perspective_options.organizing_principle: Preserve S1.1–S1.4 on design, learned recognition, signal-to-task matching and evaluation, followed by S2.1–S2.4 on drug measurement, nanomedicine components, temporal exposure and interpretive limits.
perspective_options.why_timely: The supplied outline identifies an unresolved assessment need: distinguishing computational contributions and laboratory measurement results from evidence for reliable exposure characterization; no recent field-wide development has been verified.
perspective_options.contribution: The intended contribution is a connected assessment linking physical sensing processes, computational outputs, evaluation units and exposure interpretation. Whether existing reviews already provide this synthesis remains to be checked.
competing_positions: Studies with matched simpler comparators may find no incremental benefit from AI, or may find that preprocessing or sensor chemistry explains apparent gains.
Independent evaluations may establish robust transfer across specimens, matrices, batches or time, challenging an overly restrictive assessment of generalizability.
Independent evaluations may instead show performance loss or leakage-sensitive results, challenging claims of reliable recognition or concentration estimation.
Validated reference comparisons and longitudinal measurements may support exposure claims beyond isolated laboratory demonstrations; their absence must not be assumed.
Some relevant sensing tasks may be adequately addressed by conventional calibration, whereas others may require learned interpretation of overlapping or multidimensional responses.
risks: Direct anticancer-drug exposure studies combining a functional nanosensing component and a substantive AI contribution may be sparse.
Broad methodological evidence from Chapter 1 could be incorrectly presented as direct evidence for anticancer-drug exposure in Chapter 2.
Terminology may obscure whether a system measures a drug, a carrier-associated label, a surrogate or a model-derived quantity.
Overlapping subsection topics require explicit assignment rules to prevent duplicated study summaries.
No subsection word targets are present in the supplied outline object; chapter allocations cannot be checked against the journal's full-review word limit.

inclusion.reason: Enables assessment of evidence progression without equating simplified and clinical matrices.

selection_criteria.time_window: Provisional: no lower publication-date cutoff; search through the actual final search date, which must be recorded when searching occurs.
languages: No language restriction at discovery; interpretation requires source text accessible to the research team or a reliable translation. Unassessable records remain pending rather than scientifically excluded.
source_types: Reviews and perspectives for context and citation discovery
Published conference abstracts, with abstract-level claim limits
selection_criteria.preprint_policy: Preprints may be included and must be flagged; they may not be the sole support for a major point. Link subsequent published versions and document material differences.
significance_signals: A clearly documented methodological advance with experimental evaluation of a model-recommended sensing component or condition.
A comparison that isolates the incremental contribution of AI against matched conventional calibration or simpler models.
Independent evaluation across biological specimens, individuals, matrices, sensor batches, laboratories or time.
Explicitly characterized drug identity, concentration measurand, matrix and independent analytical reference.
Evidence distinguishing carrier-associated signals from intact carrier, payload or released drug.
Longitudinal measurements or temporally separated validation that distinguish observations from model-derived exposure estimates.
A strong null, negative, replication or contrary result that materially changes interpretation of reliability.
A methodological analysis exposing evaluation-unit errors, data leakage or unsupported exposure inferences.

primary_themes.name: AI-assisted design and optimization of sensors and probes
primary_themes.scope: How are computational models used to select or optimize the physical components of a nanosensing system? Discuss relevant examples of selecting sensing materials, surface chemistry or recognition elements. Discuss relevant examples of designing or optimizing probe sequences. Discuss relevant examples of selecting complementary components for sensor arrays. Discuss relevant examples of optimizing fabrication or measurement conditions. Explain what enters the model, what it predicts or recommends, and whether the recommendation was experimentally evaluated. Distinguish designing a sensing component from selecting useful features in measurements already collected.
primary_themes.includes: materials; surface chemistry; recognition elements; probe sequences; array components; fabrication and measurement conditions
primary_themes.excludes: feature selection on already collected measurements; drug-delivery design without a sensing function; Drug-delivery design, unless it directly involves a sensing function.

primary_themes.name: From individual recognition events to learned molecular fingerprints
primary_themes.scope: How can models interpret patterns across sensor responses to recognize analytes or characterize biological samples? Explain machine perception through the relationship between interactions at the sensing surface, the resulting spectral or multisensor response, the features used by the computational model, and the predicted analyte identity, concentration category or sample characteristic. Clarify how this differs from interpreting a single sensor response through a conventional calibration relationship.
primary_themes.includes: spectral fingerprints; multisensor arrays; pattern recognition
primary_themes.excludes: Implying that learned recognition eliminates the importance of sensor chemistry.; Implying that a predictive fingerprint necessarily establishes its biological mechanism.

primary_themes.name: Matching learning tasks to biosensor signals
primary_themes.scope: Which computational tasks suit different biosensor signals, and why? Organize the discussion around signal, then analytical task, then method, then output. Optical or Raman spectra: preprocessing, denoising, feature extraction, classification and concentration estimation. Multisensor-array fingerprints: analyte discrimination, pattern recognition and multianalyte analysis. Electrochemical responses: calibration, interference discrimination and concentration estimation. Repeated measurements: drift correction, tracking and temporal prediction. Explain model families only where they clarify an included study. Distinguish exploratory dimensionality reduction from predictive classification or regression. Compare with simpler analytical approaches where the evidence permits.
primary_themes.includes: optical and Raman spectra; multisensor arrays; electrochemical responses; repeated measurements
primary_themes.excludes: Assuming that greater model complexity means better performance.

primary_themes.name: Interpreting performance and generalization
primary_themes.scope: What does a reported performance result establish, and under which evaluation conditions? Distinguish analytical performance: measurement accuracy, precision, selectivity and useful concentration range. Distinguish predictive performance: classification or regression performance on appropriately separated evaluation data. Distinguish generalization: performance across new biological samples, individuals, matrices, sensor batches or time points. Identify the independent evaluation unit. Introduce these evaluation principles here; their consequences for drug-exposure measurement belong to Chapter 2.
primary_themes.includes: analytical performance; predictive performance; generalization; evaluation units
primary_themes.excludes: Describing multiple spectra from one specimen as multiple independent biological samples.

primary_themes.name: Identifying anticancer drugs and estimating their concentrations
primary_themes.scope: What drug-related information do AI-enabled nanosensing systems actually produce? Distinguish detecting drug presence, identifying a drug, classifying a concentration into categories, and estimating a numerical concentration. For the selected studies, connect the drug, sensing mechanism, biological matrix, computational task and evaluation result. Separate experiments in buffer, synthetic biofluids, spiked biological specimens and specimens collected after administration. Where reported, identify the reference analytical method. Where reported, distinguish parent drug from metabolites, and total from unbound concentration.
primary_themes.includes: anticancer drugs; biological matrices; reference methods
primary_themes.excludes: Describing concentration classification as continuous quantitative measurement.; Describing synthetic-fluid performance as established patient performance.

primary_themes.name: Measuring nanomedicines: carrier, payload and release
primary_themes.scope: When a nanomedicine is sensed, which component or process does the signal represent? A carrier-associated label does not by itself establish intact-carrier abundance, released drug concentration, or biologically available payload. Distinguish measurements of the nanocarrier or a carrier-associated signal, of the drug payload, of encapsulated and released drug, and of release-related changes or distribution. Explain the specific contribution of AI to interpreting these measurements. Evaluate whether sensing supplies feedback for assessing or refining a delivery system.
primary_themes.excludes: treatment selection; dose adjustment; Inferring a demonstrated feedback loop merely because AI was used to design the formulation.; Detailed treatment selection and dose-adjustment strategies.

primary_themes.name: From individual measurements to exposure over time
primary_themes.scope: How can sensor measurements support temporal exposure assessment, and which parts are measured versus modeled? Distinguish single measurements, serial sampling, continuous or near-continuous sensing, pharmacokinetic estimation and prediction of future concentrations. When measurements are coupled to pharmacokinetic or machine-learning models, identify the observations supplied to the model, the quantities estimated, the assumptions required, and how temporal predictions were evaluated. Address sampling frequency, response lag, reversibility, drift and recalibration where relevant.
primary_themes.includes: serial and continuous sensing; pharmacokinetic models; temporal prediction
primary_themes.excludes: Treating repeated technical measurements as longitudinal monitoring.; Presenting a predicted concentration-time curve as continuously measured data.

primary_themes.name: Limits to interpreting measured concentrations as biological exposure
primary_themes.scope: What prevents the reported measurements from supporting broader exposure claims? Synthesize limitations demonstrated or left unresolved by the selected evidence: matrix interference and sample preparation; transfer across drugs, specimens, individuals and sensor batches; limited concentration ranges or temporal evaluation; differences between the sampled compartment and the tumour; missing independent reference measurements. Explain the consequence of each limitation. Distinguish not investigated, insufficiently reported, and tested with poor performance. Close with what the selected evidence supports and what remains necessary for reliable exposure assessment.
primary_themes.includes: matrix effects; transferability; compartment versus tumour; reference measurements

assumptions: The supplied researcher_outline object is the operative outline. Its subsection questions and exclusions are fixed; no alternative perspective or primary-theme structure is proposed.

For topic boundaries, nanobiosensing provisionally requires a nanoscale component with a functional sensing role, not merely a nanoscale delivery vehicle. A biological recognition element is not mandatory for chemical drug-sensing platforms relevant to the outline.

For topic boundaries, no organism or matrix restriction is imposed. Chapter 1 may draw on directly relevant methods outside anticancer-drug sensing, but such evidence does not establish Chapter 2 exposure performance.
For topic boundaries, discovery has no lower date cutoff or language restriction. The final search date and any practical translation limitations must be recorded during literature work.
For audience readiness, the journal's non-specialist scientific readership is adopted because the researcher supplied no narrower audience.

For competing-position readiness, the listed challenges are provisional screening targets rather than verified positions in the literature; their actual presence and evidential support require literature inspection.

AI terminology is treated broadly enough for discovery to capture machine learning, learned chemometric models and model-guided optimization. Conventional calibration and exploratory dimensionality reduction remain explicit comparators and must not automatically be relabeled as AI-enabled prediction.
Reference methods and conventional sensors may be retained as direct comparators or methodological context even when they do not themselves contain nanoscale or AI components.
No chapter or subsection word allocations are inferred: the supplied outline object contains none, and the journal's 5,000-word limit applies to the full review.
questions_for_researcher: The supplied outline object contains no word targets. What combined or chapter-level word allocation should the first two chapters use within the full review's 5,000-word main-text limit?

primary_themes.name: S1.1 — AI-assisted design and optimization of sensors and probes
primary_themes.scope: How computational models select or optimize physical sensing components or experimental conditions.
primary_themes.includes: Materials, surface chemistry, recognition elements, probe sequences, complementary array components, fabrication and measurement conditions; model inputs, recommendations and experimental evaluation.
primary_themes.excludes: Feature selection from already collected measurements; delivery design without sensing; downstream recognition performance except where needed to evaluate a design recommendation.

primary_themes.name: S1.2 — From individual recognition events to learned molecular fingerprints
primary_themes.scope: How surface interactions and collective sensor responses become learned analyte or sample representations.
primary_themes.includes: Spectral and multisensor fingerprints; links among sensing chemistry, measured response, computational features and predicted identity, concentration category or sample characteristic; contrasts with single-response calibration.
primary_themes.excludes: Physical component optimization assigned to T1; general algorithm descriptions without a recognition connection; claims that predictive fingerprints alone establish mechanism.

primary_themes.name: S1.3 — Matching learning tasks to biosensor signals
primary_themes.scope: Which analytical tasks and computational methods suit particular signal types and outputs.
primary_themes.includes: Optical and Raman preprocessing, denoising and feature extraction; classification and regression; multisensor discrimination and multianalyte analysis; electrochemical calibration and interference discrimination; drift correction, tracking and temporal prediction methods; simpler comparators.
primary_themes.excludes: Exploratory dimensionality reduction described as validated prediction; drug-exposure conclusions without evidence assigned to Chapter 2; general method catalogues unrelated to included signals.

primary_themes.name: S1.4 — Interpreting performance and generalization
primary_themes.scope: What analytical and predictive results establish under their evaluation designs.
primary_themes.includes: Accuracy, precision, selectivity, concentration range, classification and regression evaluation, independent evaluation units, specimen-level separation, leakage, external evaluation and transfer across individuals, matrices, batches or time.
primary_themes.excludes: Drug-exposure-specific consequences, assigned to T8; treating multiple measurements from one specimen as independent biological samples.

primary_themes.name: S2.1 — Identifying anticancer drugs and estimating their concentrations
primary_themes.scope: What drug-related information nanosensing systems produce and how it is evaluated.
primary_themes.includes: Presence detection, drug identification, concentration categories and numerical concentration estimates; sensing mechanism, biological matrix, computational task, evaluation and reference method; parent drug versus metabolites and total versus unbound concentration where reported.
primary_themes.excludes: Carrier and release-specific interpretation assigned to T6; longitudinal exposure inference assigned to T7; equating synthetic-fluid results with patient performance.

primary_themes.name: S2.2 — Measuring nanomedicines: carrier, payload and release
primary_themes.scope: Which nanomedicine component or process an observed signal represents and what AI contributes to interpreting it.
primary_themes.includes: Carrier-associated signals, intact-carrier measurements, payload, encapsulated and released drug, release-related changes and distribution; demonstrated sensing feedback used to assess or refine delivery systems.
primary_themes.excludes: Formulation optimization without sensing; inference of released or biologically available payload from carrier labels alone; detailed treatment selection and dose adjustment.

primary_themes.name: S2.3 — From individual measurements to exposure over time
primary_themes.scope: How observations support temporal exposure estimates and how measured quantities differ from modeled quantities.
primary_themes.includes: Single measurements as contrasted with serial sampling, continuous or near-continuous sensing, pharmacokinetic estimation and future-concentration prediction; model observations, estimates, assumptions and temporal validation; sampling frequency, lag, reversibility, drift and recalibration.
primary_themes.excludes: Technical repetition characterized as longitudinal monitoring; predicted concentration-time curves characterized as continuously measured data; treatment decisions.

primary_themes.name: S2.4 — Limits to interpreting measured concentrations as biological exposure
primary_themes.scope: Consequences of demonstrated or unresolved measurement limitations for broader exposure claims.
primary_themes.includes: Matrix interference, sample preparation, transfer across drugs and specimens, individuals and batches, concentration and temporal coverage, sampled-compartment versus tumour exposure and independent reference measurements; distinctions among not investigated, insufficiently reported and tested with poor performance.
primary_themes.excludes: Standalone generic evaluation principles assigned to T4; unsupported assertions that an unreported measurement failed; detailed response, toxicity or treatment-decision discussions.

theme_framework_proposed_by_A02.count_justification: Eight primary themes reproduce the eight supplied subsections exactly. S1 and S2 are parent chapters, not additional themes. Records may receive multiple theme assignments when they answer distinct subsection questions; shared evidence should be synthesized without duplicating paper summaries.

Presenting a predicted concentration-time curve as continuously measured data.

sections.heading: Limits to interpreting measured concentrations as biological exposure
questions: What prevents the reported measurements from supporting broader exposure claims?
guidance: Synthesize limitations demonstrated or left unresolved by the selected evidence: matrix interference and sample preparation; transfer across drugs, specimens, individuals and sensor batches; limited concentration ranges or temporal evaluation; differences between the sampled compartment and the tumour; missing independent reference measurements.
Explain the consequence of each limitation.
Distinguish not investigated, insufficiently reported, and tested with poor performance.
Close with what the selected evidence supports and what remains necessary for reliable exposure assessment.
